content.title: About
content.content: A custard-filled doughnut with icing is a sweet fried pastry shaped like a ring, filled with smooth custard and topped with a glossy icing. The dough is typically made from wheat flour, yeast, milk, eggs and sugar, then deep‑fried until golden.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts became popular in the United States in the 19th century after originating in Europe.
The custard filling is often made from egg yolks, sugar and milk, giving it a silky texture.
Icing can be chocolate, vanilla or fruit‑flavored, depending on preference.
Traditional toppings include sprinkles, nuts or fresh berries.
In many countries doughnuts are enjoyed with hot coffee or tea as a morning snack.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: The carbohydrate and sugar content provides a rapid boost of energy.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: Milk and cream used in the dough and custard supply calcium for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast and eggs add B1, B2 and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive sugar in the icing and custard can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Saturated and trans fats
items.content: Deep‑frying adds saturated fats and sometimes trans fats, which are best limited.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Doughnuts may contain milk, eggs, wheat and nuts (if used in the icing), which are common allergens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Doughnuts are usually served at room temperature. They can be eaten as a standalone treat, split open for extra filling, or paired with a hot beverage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep doughnuts in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑lock bag and reheat in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Escargot are edible land snails that have long been a culinary delicacy, especially in France. They have a delicate, slightly nutty flavor and a tender, slightly springy texture. Escargot are commonly served as an appetizer and used in salads, pastas, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Escargot have been eaten since ancient Rome and Egypt.
France celebrates a "Fête de l'Escargot" dedicated to this delicacy.
Edible snails are farmed on specialized farms where their diet and environment are carefully controlled.
There are over 500 species of land snails, but only a few dozen are used in cuisine.
Traditional preparation involves cleaning, simmering in wine with herbs, then sautéing in butter with garlic and parsley.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Escargot provide about 13 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good source of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many seafood items, snails are low in fat and calories.

items.title: Source of iron and vitamin B12
items.content: They supply iron and vitamin B12, essential for blood formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals support muscle and heart function.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: A modest amount of omega‑3 contributes to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mollusks and snails.

items.title: Parasites
items.content: Raw snails can harbor parasites, so thorough cooking is required.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Traditional recipes often use salt and sauces, increasing sodium intake.

items.title: Heavy metals
items.content: Snails can accumulate toxins from polluted environments; purchase from reputable farms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Escargot are usually served as an appetizer: they are cleaned, simmered in wine with herbs, then sautéed in butter with garlic and parsley. They can be added to pasta, risotto, salads, or used as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh snail meat should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 2 days. Frozen escargot retain quality for up to 6 months at –18 °C. Thaw in the fridge before cooking and rinse under running water.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat loaf made with ham is a baked dish prepared from ground meat (usually beef or pork), finely diced ham, eggs, breadcrumbs and seasonings. It has a dense texture, a fragrant ham flavor and a tender taste, suitable as a main course or a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of making meat loaf dates back to medieval Europe, where it was known as "pot-loaf".
Ham in the recipe adds not only flavor but also extra moisture to the finished loaf.
Meat loaf is often served with gravy or tomato sauce.
In some regions it is glazed with ketchup or barbecue sauce for a sweet‑savory finish.
The dish slices easily into portions, making it popular for picnics and school lunches.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The ground meat and ham provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ham and meat are abundant in vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: When balanced with lean meat, the loaf can provide beneficial monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Large amounts of meat and ham can raise saturated fat levels, which may be undesirable for heart‑related conditions.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Ham often contains added salt and nitrites; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked ground meat may harbor pathogens; ensure the loaf reaches an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergy or intolerance to certain types of meat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the meat loaf into thick or thin pieces and serve hot or cold. It pairs well with mustard, gravy, tomato sauce, or simply as a sandwich filling. Complement with mashed potatoes, vegetable sides and fresh salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked loaf to room temperature, then wrap tightly in plastic film or place in an airtight container. Store in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑sized slices – up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen baked potato fries are pre‑cut strips that are blanched, flash‑frozen, and ready to bake in the oven. When baked they develop a crispy golden exterior while staying soft inside. The product is convenient to store in the freezer and can be prepared quickly without added oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen french fries first appeared in the United States in the 1950s as a fast‑food convenience.
A light coating of vegetable oil and special batter mixes are often used to achieve a crunchy crust.
French fries are one of the most popular side dishes worldwide, especially in fast‑food restaurants.
Rapid‑freeze technology helps retain much of the flavor and nutrients of the potatoes.
In many countries fries are served with ketchup, mayonnaise, cheese sauce, or a variety of seasonings.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Despite heat processing, some vitamin C remains, providing antioxidant benefits.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: When made from whole potatoes, fries contain dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Potatoes provide a quick source of carbohydrates useful for replenishing energy after physical activity.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: Baked fries prepared without hydrogenated oils do not contain trans fats.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: French fries are calorie‑dense due to carbs and sometimes added oil; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: They are often salted, which can increase sodium intake and affect blood pressure.

items.title: Acrylamide
items.content: Prolonged baking at high temperatures can form acrylamide, a potential toxin; aim for a golden, not dark, crust.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to potatoes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bake the fries in a preheated oven at 200 °C for 12‑15 minutes until golden and crisp. Serve hot with your favorite sauces such as ketchup, mayo, cheese sauce, garlic aioli, or sprinkle with seasonings. They can also be added to salads, tacos, or used as a side for meat dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen fries in an airtight bag in the freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, cook immediately and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Tapioca pudding is a ready‑to‑eat dessert made from tapioca starch derived from the cassava root. It has a smooth, slightly chewy texture, a mild sweetness, and is often flavored with vanilla, fruit pieces, or dairy additions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tapioca is extracted from the cassava plant, which is cultivated in tropical regions of Asia, Africa and South America.
It is naturally gluten‑free, making it suitable for gluten‑free diets.
Traditional Thai “tapioca with coconut milk” uses the same base ingredients but is prepared at home.
Tapioca pudding is usually served chilled, though it can be gently warmed.
Tapioca starch has a high thickening power, allowing the pudding to set quickly when cooled.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Tapioca contains virtually no fat, making the pudding a light dessert option.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The starch provides a quick source of energy, useful for active individuals.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Tapioca is considered hypoallergenic and rarely triggers food reactions.

items.title: Fortification potential
items.content: Ready‑to‑eat versions are often fortified with vitamins and minerals such as calcium and vitamin D.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Tapioca can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, so people with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Many commercial puddings contain significant amounts of sugar; choose low‑sugar options when possible.

items.title: Cassava allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may be allergic to cassava or its derivatives.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some products may contain artificial flavors, preservatives, or colorings.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The pudding is ready to eat straight from the container. It can be enjoyed chilled, topped with fresh berries, sliced fruit, nuts, or a sprinkle of cinnamon. If preferred, it can be gently warmed, which will soften the texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the pudding refrigerated at 2‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may become grainy.

content.title: About
content.content: Stevia powder is a natural sweetener derived from the leaves of the Stevia rebaudiana plant. The powder is intensely sweet (up to 300‑400 times sweeter than sugar) while providing virtually zero calories and a low glycemic index. It is used in cooking, baking, beverages, and diet recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stevia originates from South America, where indigenous peoples used it long before colonization.
Its sweetness comes from steviol glycosides, which are not metabolized by the human body.
Unlike sugar, stevia does not raise blood glucose levels, making it suitable for people with diabetes.
Stevia has been granted GRAS status in the US and approved by EFSA in Europe.
The powder dissolves easily in hot and cold liquids, though high amounts may leave a slight aftertaste.

items.title: Low Calorie
items.content: Stevia provides virtually no calories, helping to control overall energy intake.

items.title: Blood Sugar Support
items.content: Steviol glycosides do not cause glucose spikes, which is beneficial for pre‑diabetes and type 2 diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidant Properties
items.content: Steviol glycosides exhibit antioxidant activity, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Blood Pressure Reduction
items.content: Some studies suggest regular stevia consumption may contribute to modest blood pressure lowering.

items.title: Oral Health
items.content: Stevia does not promote tooth decay and may reduce bacterial growth in the mouth.

items.title: Allergic Reactions
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergy to stevia; discontinue use if symptoms appear.

items.title: Aftertaste
items.content: High doses can produce a bitter or licorice‑like aftertaste that not everyone finds pleasant.

items.title: Medication Interactions
items.content: Stevia may enhance the effect of antihypertensive drugs; consult a physician if you take such medication.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add stevia powder to tea, coffee, smoothies, yogurts, sauces, and baked goods. When substituting sugar, a typical ratio is 1 g stevia to 10 g sugar, but adjust to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store stevia powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For extended shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and flavor loss.
